rationale: Exodus 12 commands Israel to "remove the leaven from your houses" for the seven days of Unleavened Bread (12:15, BSB) and adds, "For seven days there must be no leaven found in your houses" (12:19). The Septuagint (Swete, on Bible Hub) uses the same noun, zyme, at 12:15 and 12:19 that Matthew uses at 16:6-12. Commentators read on Bible Hub trace the negative sense of leaven to these Passover rules: the Pulpit Commentary on 16:6 says leaven was "regarded as a sign of impurity and corruption, we learn from the strict rules which banished it from Divine service, and especially during the Passover season," and the Cambridge Bible on 13:33 says the use of leaven for "the working of evil" "probably arose from the prohibition of leaven during the paschal season." Paul makes the Passover link explicitly in 1 Corinthians 5:7-8 ("Get rid of the old leaven ... For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed," BSB). The motif is a recurring image, following conn-matt14-feeding-exodus16, where an Old Testament background named by commentators but not by Matthew is graded motif/plausible, and the grade stays plausible because Matthew 16 has no Passover vocabulary, no citation and no reference to Exodus: the background is the commentators' inference, and Ellicott on 13:33 points out that leaven was also baked into the firstfruits loaves offered at Pentecost (Leviticus 23:17). The connection does not grade the meaning of "leaven" in 13:33, which is disputed in the lesson's Positions.
